nutritionExperience.comebackBody: A date without a check-in does not erase your earlier dinners. Returning counts.
nutritionExperience.continueWeek: Continue my week of real dinners
nutritionExperience.cueBody: Serve dinner as the sun goes down, between 6:00 and 7:30 PM, or at least 2.5 to 3 hours before bed. Closing the digestive cycle early clears the way for melatonin and deep rest.
nutritionExperience.cycleRecordedBody: You earned 10 points for this date. Eating a larger dinner gives no extra points.

nutritionExperience.intro: An early dinner, cooked clean and built by proportions, so eating well stops being a decision you make all over again every night.
nutritionExperience.metaDescription: Have dinner as the sun goes down and build your plate by proportions with what is harvested nearby.
nutritionExperience.metaTitle: Nutrition ritual: A real, local dinner at sunset
nutritionExperience.minimumBody: Half the plate in seasonal vegetables —that is where “one more plant” lives—, a quarter protein and a quarter carbohydrate from your region, plus one portion of healthy fat. Eyeball it: we do not measure calories, weight or portions.
nutritionExperience.minimumCheckbox: I served the triad with one more plant
nutritionExperience.noHabitClaim: Five times do not prove that you formed a habit; they are five pieces of evidence that you can make choosing real, fresh, local food easy.
nutritionExperience.preparationBody: Bringing the week’s fresh food from a market or a street market, in bulk and in your own jars, reduces friction and rubbish. It is a recommendation, never a requirement for your dinner to count.
nutritionExperience.preparationTitle: Stock up close to home, not an exam
nutritionExperience.publicCardBody: cultivated their first real dinner in A real, local dinner at sunset.
nutritionExperience.publicCardTitle: {name} made a real, local dinner easy
nutritionExperience.publicFinalCardBody: cultivated five real dinners in A real, local dinner at sunset.
nutritionExperience.publicLink: See A real, local dinner at sunset
nutritionExperience.ritualBody: Six steps that hold each other up: each one takes friction out of the next, and only the two anchors make the dinner count.
nutritionExperience.ritualStep1: Stock up close to home: a market, a street market or a small producer; in season, in bulk and with your own bags and jars.
nutritionExperience.ritualStep2: Set the time anchor: have dinner as the sun goes down, between 6:00 and 7:30 PM.
nutritionExperience.ritualStep3: Cook clean: steam, air fryer or homemade broth; if you sauté, a few drops of avocado or extra virgin olive oil.
nutritionExperience.ritualStep4: Serve the triad: half the plate in local vegetables —that is where “one more plant” goes—, a quarter protein and a quarter carbohydrate from your region, plus a healthy fat.
nutritionExperience.ritualStep5: Eat present: no screens, chewing slowly and recognising where each thing came from.
nutritionExperience.ritualStep6: Notice the triple impact next morning: lightness on waking, less rubbish at home and your local economy kept alive.
nutritionExperience.ritualTitle: Stock up, anchor, cook, serve, be present and notice
nutritionExperience.safety: This practice does not prescribe a diet or replace clinical advice. Adapt it to your allergies, intolerances, work schedule and access, and to guidance from your health professionals.

mindExperience.celebrationBody: You opened the day screen-free and gave someone real presence, without waiting for the perfect moment.
mindExperience.comebackBody: One noisy day does not erase the calm ones before it. Coming back to the pause counts.
mindExperience.comebackTitle: Coming back to calm counts too
mindExperience.cueBody: Leave the first 30 to 60 minutes of the day without social media, notifications or news. That stretch is for breathing, stretching or simply being. Charging your phone outside the bedroom makes it almost automatic.
mindExperience.cycleRecordedBody: You earned 10 points for this date. Points count days, never how many people or how much time.
mindExperience.finalBody: You reached the flexible goal of five days, without measuring how many people, how long or how well it went.

mindExperience.incomplete: Confirm that you opened the day screen-free and gave someone your presence.
mindExperience.intro: A stretch of silence as the day opens and one real conversation, so calm and connection stop depending on having time left over.
mindExperience.metaDescription: Open the day screen-free and give someone real presence, face to face where you can.
mindExperience.metaTitle: Mind and spirit ritual: Presence, peace and local connection
mindExperience.minimumBody: Give one person real presence: face to face where you can and with no devices in sight —at the table, with a neighbour, with whoever sells to you at the market—. If there is nobody near you today, a call or an honest message counts just the same: what counts is really listening, not the channel.
mindExperience.noHabitClaim: Five times do not prove that you formed a habit; they are five pieces of evidence that calm and connection fit into your day.
mindExperience.preparationBody: Charging your phone outside the bedroom and keeping a corner with natural light removes almost all the friction. It is a recommendation, never a requirement for your day to count.
mindExperience.preparationTitle: Set the calm up, not an exam
mindExperience.publicCardBody: held their first day of presence with Presence, peace and local connection.
mindExperience.publicCardEyebrow: Presence that returns to what is close
mindExperience.publicFinalCardBody: held five days of presence with Presence, peace and local connection.
mindExperience.publicFinalCardTitle: {name} reached their harvest of present days
mindExperience.publicLink: See Presence, peace and local connection
mindExperience.ritualBody: Five steps that fit into an ordinary day. Only the two anchors make the day count; the other three add a lot and are free.
mindExperience.ritualStep1: Open the day screen-free: the first 30 to 60 minutes with no social media, notifications or news.
mindExperience.ritualStep2: Step outside for air: 10 to 15 minutes of light, soil or grass. It is the same time outdoors the Movement pillar already asks for, not an extra trip.
mindExperience.ritualStep3: Have a real conversation with someone: face to face and with no devices in sight, listening without preparing your reply.
mindExperience.ritualStep4: Close with gratitude or with a gesture: three things you are grateful for in your surroundings, or a hand offered to someone who lives nearby.
mindExperience.ritualStep5: Notice the triple impact next day: calm on waking, a quieter home and a neighbourhood where you now know one more person.
mindExperience.ritualTitle: Be quiet, step out, talk, give thanks and notice
mindExperience.safety: This practice keeps you company, it does not treat you. If anxiety, sadness or loneliness hold on over time, asking for professional help is also caring for your mind, and it is the right thing to do. Respect limits, privacy and availability: nobody is obliged to take up a bond that does not feel safe.

movementExperience.ritualStep1: Head out without an engine: the short errand, on foot or by bike, with your legs or your own propulsion.
movementExperience.ritualStep2: Two minutes on your feet for every 50 in a chair: squats, calf raises, hip and thoracic mobility.
movementExperience.ritualStep3: 20 to 30 minutes outdoors, on soil, grass or a trail, to get direct sunlight and wake the foot up.

movementExperience.ritualStep5: Notice the triple impact next day: vitality in the body, fuel you did not spend and neighbours you actually ran into.
movementExperience.ritualTitle: Head out, pause, get sun, get strong and notice
movementExperience.safety: Adapt movement to your capacity, your space and your supports: if you use a wheelchair, crutches or a cane, your way of getting around counts the same. Stop if something does not feel safe and follow guidance from your health professionals.

atomicSleepChallenge.morningDate: Local morning date that closed the cycle
atomicSleepChallenge.morningDescription: Within the first hour after waking, step outside for 10 to 15 minutes of natural light, without sunglasses and without looking straight at the sun. That light sets your body clock and schedules tonight’s melatonin.
atomicSleepChallenge.nightCheckbox: I parked my devices and dimmed the lights
atomicSleepChallenge.nightDescription: An hour before bed, put screens out of reach and turn the lights down. Bright light at night holds melatonin back and tells your brain it is still midday.
atomicSleepChallenge.noHabitClaim: Five times are not enough to claim you formed a habit; they are five pieces of evidence that you can protect your rest.
atomicSleepChallenge.recommendedBody: Five steps that fit into any ordinary night. Only the two anchors make the cycle count; the other three take friction away and are free.
atomicSleepChallenge.recommendedHeading: Close the day and open it with light
atomicSleepChallenge.ritualStep1: Anchor the morning with sun: 10 to 15 minutes of natural light in the first hour after waking, without sunglasses and without looking straight at the sun.
atomicSleepChallenge.ritualStep2: Close things down digitally and dim the house an hour before bed: screens out of reach and warm, indirect light.
atomicSleepChallenge.ritualStep3: Empty your mind onto paper: five minutes writing tomorrow’s tasks and whatever is going round in your head, so it does not come to bed with you.
atomicSleepChallenge.ritualStep4: Step into a cool, dark, well-aired room, with the phone charging outside the bedroom.
atomicSleepChallenge.ritualStep5: Notice the clarity on waking: how rested you feel and how much caffeine you actually need.
atomicSleepChallenge.safety: Light is taken outdoors and never by looking straight at the sun. Adapt movement to your capacity. If insomnia holds on over time, or if you snore or stop breathing while asleep, take it to a health professional: there are sleep disorders no ritual can fix.

mindSpirit.heading: Mind, Spirit and the Community Next Door
mindSpirit.subtitle: Getting back silence, presence and the people who live nearby.
mindSpirit.breakHeading: The Digital Revolution and Urbanisation (20th–21st century): Goodbye to the Tribe
mindSpirit.breakIntro: Before this, human beings never lived alone. «Loneliness» was a biological death sentence. Spirit and mind were fed by ritual, by the silence of nature and by the support of the group.
mindSpirit.changeText: We went from the «village» (where everyone knew each other) to the anonymous big city, and finally to the digital hyper-link (social media) that connects us with thousands while isolating us physically from everyone.
mindSpirit.impactText: Chronic loneliness appeared. The brain reads isolation as constant danger and fires up anxiety. We lost rites of passage and contact with the earth (natural spirituality), replacing them with the mental «noise» of constant comparison and empty productivity.
mindSpirit.mismatchHeading: The «Evolutionary Mismatch» in Mind and Spirit
mindSpirit.mismatchIntro: Your brain still expects to look someone in the eye while you talk, to be recognised by your community for what you do, and to feel part of something larger than yourself (nature or purpose).
mindSpirit.offer2: News bulletins full of fear instead of stories around a fire.
mindSpirit.offer3: Fierce competition instead of tribal collaboration.
mindSpirit.hiddenCostIntro: Being always available did not come free. An environment of constant stimulation, comparison and bad news charges you three things, and none of them feels like a cost while it is happening.
mindSpirit.overloadText: A nervous system with no rest, spending the day on alert and no longer able to hold attention on one thing long enough to enjoy it.
mindSpirit.uprootText: You know what is happening ten thousand kilometres away and stop recognising whoever lives nearby: the sense of belonging with neighbours and with the nature of your own territory fades.
mindSpirit.lonelinessText: Hundreds of quick interactions a day that feed neither affection nor empathy. You can be surrounded by contacts and have nobody to call on an ordinary Tuesday.
mindSpirit.localSolutionHeading: The counterweight: silence, presence and people nearby
mindSpirit.localSolutionText: Setting windows of silence, stepping out for air and really talking with whoever is beside you gives all three back at once. You do not need to disconnect from the world: you need the world to stop being on top of you all day, and the people on your street to have a face and a name again.
mindSpirit.windowsIntro: Three stretches of the day where the phone is not there. They are not minutes to count: they are prepared ground, so calm does not depend on willpower.
mindSpirit.windowMorningBody: 30 to 60 minutes with no social media, notifications or news. What gets into your head on waking sets the tone for the whole day, and the world’s news can wait until you are awake.
mindSpirit.windowTableBody: Phone off the table, face down or in another room. It is the stretch where a real conversation already fits without scheduling anything, and where presence shows up fastest.
mindSpirit.windowNightBody: The last hour screen-free, with the phone charging outside the bedroom. It is the same boundary that protects sleep in Pillar 1: late light and stimulation push deep rest back.
mindSpirit.groundingIntro: Silence alone is not enough: a head that goes still starts to ruminate. Stepping out and breathing gives it something concrete to do while it settles.
mindSpirit.groundingOutdoorBody: 10 to 15 minutes in the nearest park, garden or trail: light on your face, feet on soil or grass, and the sound of the place where you live. It is the same time outdoors the Movement pillar already asks for, not one more outing to schedule.
mindSpirit.groundingBreathIntro: Four rounds are enough, and you can do it sitting anywhere:
mindSpirit.groundingBreathIn: Breathe in through the nose while you count to 4.
mindSpirit.groundingBreathHold: Hold the air while you count to 7.
mindSpirit.groundingBreathOut: Let it out through the mouth, slowly, while you count to 8.
mindSpirit.groundingBreathNote: What calms you is breathing slowly; counting is only the way to get there without thinking about it. If it makes you dizzy, shorten the counts and keep whatever rhythm you can hold: bringing the number of breaths per minute down is what slows the pulse, not hitting an exact 4-7-8.

mindSpirit.catalogDigitalBody: Lowers comparison anxiety, gives back the ability to concentrate and protects the deep sleep of Pillar 1.

mindSpirit.catalogNatureItem3: Direct contact with soil or grass, barefoot for a while.
mindSpirit.catalogNatureItem4: Working in a garden or caring for plants.
mindSpirit.catalogNatureBody: Calms the nervous system, lowers cortisol and cuts through thoughts that keep going round in circles.
mindSpirit.catalogNatureLocal: Wakes up appreciation for the nearby ecosystem and gives reasons to preserve the green spaces of the neighbourhood.

mindSpirit.catalogDialogueItem2: Writing down three things you are grateful for in your surroundings as the day closes.
mindSpirit.catalogDialogueItem3: Greeting and chatting with neighbours and whoever sells to you at the market.
mindSpirit.catalogDialogueItem4: Listening without preparing your reply or glancing at the phone.

mindSpirit.catalogDialogueLocal: Humanises daily life and builds the neighbourhood trust that makes people help each other without anyone organising it.

mindSpirit.catalogServiceItem2: Backing solidarity economy initiatives and local consumption.
mindSpirit.catalogServiceItem3: Giving a hand to a neighbour or to a project in the area.
mindSpirit.catalogServiceItem4: Joining a clean-up day or a craft market.
mindSpirit.catalogServiceBody: Gives a sense of purpose and belonging, cuts apathy and builds self-esteem that rests on actual deeds.
mindSpirit.catalogServiceLocal: Creates mutual support networks that hold when something goes wrong, and turn the nearby surroundings into a safe place.
mindSpirit.callout: This pillar recognises that health is not only physical. It centres on emotional regulation, mental clarity and connection with others —starting with whoever lives nearby—. «Spirit/community» health means feeling part of something larger, cultivating healthy relationships and holding a clear purpose that drives the other three pillars.

mindSpirit.bridgeIntro: These are not three more tasks. Two of these bridges are the same act you already do, told from the other pillar.
mindSpirit.bridgeSleepTitle: With Sleep: the last hour is the same boundary
mindSpirit.bridgeSleepBody: Closing the day screen-free and with your head unloaded is what protects deep sleep over there: you get to bed with nothing still running inside.
mindSpirit.bridgeNutritionTitle: With Nutrition: the table is where it happens
mindSpirit.bridgeNutritionBody: Dinner with no devices in sight is your window of silence and, at the same time, the other pillar’s moment. A real conversation already fits there without looking for a slot.
mindSpirit.bridgeMovementTitle: With Movement: stepping out calms and grounds
mindSpirit.bridgeMovementBody: The time outdoors that brings the noise in your head down is the same that wakes up the body and the foot over there. One outing serves both.

movement.heading: Natural, Local, Community Movement
movement.subtitle: Getting the body back onto the street, the trail and the neighbourhood pitch.
movement.breakHeading: The Industrial Revolution (18th–19th century): Goodbye to Movement
movement.breakIntro: Before this, most of humanity worked the land, hunted or did manual work. Movement was not «exercise», it was survival.
movement.changeText: The shift from agrarian to industrial and then post-industrial societies moved work out of open spaces and physical tasks and into indoor settings and mental tasks. A «chair and screen» job took hold, with low physical demand and long days sitting down.
movement.impactText: Structural sedentariness appeared. For the first time in history, human beings began spending 8 or 12 hours sitting or standing in one place, under roofs that hid the sun from us. With machines replacing physical effort, the door opened to chronic sedentariness and many modern diseases such as obesity and cardiovascular risk.
movement.hiddenCostHeading: The hidden cost of driving two blocks
movement.hiddenCostIntro: Sedentariness did not stop at the office chair: it followed us to the front door. Starting the car or the motorbike to reach the market, the shop or someone who lives ten minutes away is paid for three times over, and none of it shows on the receipt.
movement.fuelText: Petrol and maintenance for a trip that fitted on foot, repeated several times a week for years.
movement.airText: Emissions and noise on your own street: the one your neighbours breathe and where their children play, not a distant chimney.
movement.vitalityText: Fewer steps and less spontaneous energy expenditure —the kind that happens without meaning to—, which is exactly what keeps metabolism going through the day.
movement.localSolutionHeading: The counterweight: your territory is the place you move
movement.localSolutionText: Walking or cycling the short trips, using the trails, parks and pitches nearby, and backing the gyms, studios and classes in your neighbourhood turns your surroundings into the place where you move. You do not need to change your life: you need to stop motorising what already fitted on foot.
movement.cadenceIntro: Three frequencies, no counting of sets or kilometres. What decides the outcome is how often you come back, not how much you do in one go.
movement.cadence50Body: Squats, calf raises, hip and thoracic mobility. Breaking up the chair wakes up glutes and legs, which have been switched off for nearly an hour, and gets oxygen to your head.
movement.cadenceDayBody: On soil, grass or a trail. Direct sunlight synchronises the same body clock as Pillar 1, and uneven ground wakes up the foot and your balance.
movement.cadenceWeekTitle: Useful strength and sport with people
movement.cadenceWeekBody: Calisthenics in the park, carrying water bottles or the shopping, work in the garden, a neighbourhood match, a group walk —or the gym, studio or class in your area, which are neighbourhood businesses too and count just the same—.
movement.cadenceMoreNote: And if you can give it more time, all the better for you: the minimum is a floor, not a ceiling. The one thing that does not change is that points count days and not volume, so nobody has to compete on intensity or distance.
movement.footIntro: The foot has twenty-six bones and more than thirty joints, and it spends the day inside a narrow last on a rigid sole. Giving it work back is what holds your balance up once the ground stops being flat.
movement.footShoeTitle: What to look for in a functional shoe
movement.footShoeWide: A wide toe box: your toes have to be able to spread and bear weight, not be squeezed into a point.
movement.footShoeFlex: A flexible sole: the foot should be able to bend and feel the ground, instead of riding on a rigid platform.
movement.footShoeDrop: Zero or low drop: little or no height difference between heel and toe, so the posterior chain does its work.
movement.footTerrainTitle: And what to look for in the ground
movement.footTerrainBody: Grass, soil, sand and uneven trails force a correction at every step: they strengthen the arch, improve balance and spread out impact. Walking barefoot for a while on grass or clean soil is the simplest version and costs nothing.
movement.footTransitionNote: Change footwear gradually. A foot used to a rigid sole and a raised heel needs weeks to adapt, and rushing that transition is the most common way to get injured while trying to take care of yourself.
movement.catalogHeading: A catalogue of ways to move
movement.catalogIntro: What to do, what it does for your body and what it does for your neighbourhood. The four ways the rhythm gets filled.

movement.catalogProximityItem3: Taking the stairs instead of the lift.
movement.catalogProximityItem4: Getting off one stop early and walking the last stretch.
movement.catalogProximityBody: Keeps fat and glucose metabolism active, relieves tension in the lower back and gets the legs circulating again.
movement.catalogProximityLocal: Zero emissions on short trips, direct savings on fuel and transport, and streets with people running into each other again.

movement.catalogTerrainItem2: Shoes with a wide toe box, a flexible sole and zero or low drop.
movement.catalogTerrainItem3: Hip and ankle mobility on uneven ground or trails.
movement.catalogTerrainItem4: Walks along paths, fields or parks in your region.
movement.catalogTerrainBody: Strengthens the arch, improves balance, aligns the spine and spreads impact naturally.
movement.catalogTerrainLocal: Gives reasons to look after and preserve local trails, parks and green spaces, and does not depend on disposable plastic gear.
movement.catalogStrengthItem1: Calisthenics: push-ups, free squats, pull-ups in the park.
movement.catalogStrengthItem2: Farmer’s walk: carrying water bottles, buckets or the shopping from the market.
movement.catalogStrengthItem3: Work in the garden: hauling soil, firewood or compost.
movement.catalogStrengthItem4: A guided routine at the gym or studio in your area.
movement.catalogStrengthBody: Increases bone density, preserves muscle mass, improves grip strength and stabilises the core.
movement.catalogStrengthLocal: Uses the infrastructure that already exists, sustains the neighbourhood’s exercise businesses and, with a garden, pushes food sovereignty along.

movement.catalogEnduranceItem2: A neighbourhood football match or any team sport.
movement.catalogEnduranceItem3: Group walks with family or neighbours.
movement.catalogEnduranceItem4: Group classes —dance, boxing, functional training— at a local studio.
movement.catalogEnduranceBody: Strengthens the cardiorespiratory system, lowers cortisol levels and releases endorphins.

movement.callout: This pillar is about pushing back on sedentariness by working physical activity into daily life. It is not limited to the gym, and it does not exclude it either: it covers walking, cycling, playing football, working the land or training at a neighbourhood studio. The aim is for movement to fit back into the day, and for your surroundings —streets, trails, pitches and local businesses— to be where it happens.

movement.bridgeSleepBody: The day’s activity builds up the sleep pressure that makes you sleepy at dusk, and the outdoor light of your time outside anchors the same clock that opens your morning over there.

movement.bridgeMindBody: The 20 to 30 minutes on soil or a trail this pillar asks for are the same ones that bring the noise in your head down over there. One is enough for both.

nutrition.heading: Natural, Nourishing, Local Food
nutrition.subtitle: Reconnecting with the source, the season and the people who grow it.
nutrition.breakHeading: The Green Revolution, Ultra-Processed Food and the Global Chain (post-WWII)
nutrition.breakIntro: This is where eating broke. In the 1950s the priority was feeding a population that was exploding, and quantity won over quality: produce plenty of cheap calories and move them far.
nutrition.changeText: Refined vegetable oils appeared, along with white flour at scale, sugar in everything and a supply chain that crosses continents.
nutrition.impactText: We went from eating «food from the earth» to «edible products» designed to survive the journey: addictive, nutritionally empty and cut off from whoever grew them.
nutrition.hiddenCostHeading: The hidden cost of the global chain
nutrition.hiddenCostIntro: An imported ultra-processed product does not only arrive empty of nutrients: it arrives after thousands of kilometres. That journey is paid for three times over, and none of it shows on the label.
nutrition.transportText: Thousands of kilometres by lorry, ship and plane for every ingredient, with the fuel and the CO₂ and other greenhouse gas emissions that demands.
nutrition.packagingText: Tonnes of single-use plastic that exist so the food survives the trip and the warehouse, not so it feeds you better.
nutrition.wasteText: Spoilage and loss in transit, plus weeks in cold storage burning energy to preserve something that has already lost its nutrient density.
nutrition.localSolutionText: Buying in season and close to home reverses all three costs at once. Food is harvested ripe and arrives with its vitamins intact, middlemen and packaging fall away, the waste of the journey is cut, and the money stays with whoever grew it, a few kilometres from your table.
nutrition.evidence: Since the post-war years, the drive to produce lots of cheap calories (the Green Revolution plus food industrialisation) eased the shift towards ultra-processed food built on sugar, flour and refined oils, and towards a supply chain that moves food between continents. It solved much of acute hunger, but at the cost of diets that are less diverse and more «laboratory-made» — today strongly tied to chronic disease and environmental damage. Going back to patterns built on minimally processed, varied, seasonal and locally sourced food fits human and planetary health far better.
nutrition.callout: More than a diet, this pillar is about the connection to the source. It encourages real, seasonal, locally sourced food, and builds the bridge between the people who grow it and the people who cook it.
nutrition.triadIntro: No scales and no calorie counting: you can see the proportion. Half the plate, a quarter and a quarter, plus one portion of healthy fat, with what is harvested nearby.
nutrition.triadVegetablesBody: Vegetables freshly harvested in your region, with no plastic packaging and no long journeys: fibre, micronutrients and volume. This is where “one more plant” happens.
nutrition.triadProteinBody: Native legumes bought in bulk, free-range eggs from a nearby farm, sustainable local fish or pasture-raised poultry. Amino acids and satiety without overloading digestion at night.
nutrition.triadCarbsBody: Local root vegetables, nixtamalised native maize, native squash or whole grains in bulk. Slow-release energy and fibre that feeds the gut microbiota.
nutrition.triadFatBody: Avocado from nearby groves, seeds in bulk or an artisanal nut butter with no additives. Without them vitamins A, D, E and K are not absorbed.
nutrition.cookingIntro: Industrial seed oils —soy, maize, safflower, canola, sunflower— go through thermal and chemical refining. Heated up they produce aldehydes and pro-inflammatory compounds, and they almost always arrive bottled in plastic from far away.
nutrition.oilAvocadoUse: Medium-high heat: sautéing, roasting or griddling. Unrefined, its smoke point sits around 250 °C; the refined one reaches 271 °C, but loses on the way what we came here to protect.
nutrition.oilOliveUse: Raw or low heat: dressings and finishing. Cold-pressed and rich in polyphenols.
nutrition.cookingZeroHeading: And what needs no added fat at all
nutrition.cookingZeroBody: Steam, air fryer, homemade vegetable or bone broths, and a well pre-heated cast iron or non-stick pan. They cook just as well, avoid oxidative stress and replace a packaged purchase.

nutrition.catalogProteinsItem1: Local legumes: black, pinto or bayo beans and lentils in bulk.
nutrition.catalogProteinsItem2: Free-range eggs from a regional farm.
nutrition.catalogProteinsItem3: Sustainable local fish or pasture-raised poultry from nearby.
nutrition.catalogProteinsItem4: Artisanal tofu or locally produced tempeh.
nutrition.catalogProteinsNutrition: Complete amino acids for cell repair, lasting satiety and digestion that does not sit heavy at night.
nutrition.catalogProteinsLocal: Buying in bulk removes plastic packaging and long industrial refrigeration. The money goes straight to farming families in your area.
nutrition.catalogCarbsItem1: Sweet potato, cassava and potato from nearby growers; cooked and cooled, potato gains resistant starch.
nutrition.catalogCarbsItem2: Nixtamalised native maize: the real tortilla.
nutrition.catalogCarbsItem3: Plantain from your area and native squash.
nutrition.catalogCarbsItem4: Whole grains in bulk: oats, brown or wild rice, quinoa, millet or buckwheat.
nutrition.catalogCarbsNutrition: Slow-release energy, prebiotic fibre that feeds the microbiota, and no sharp glucose or insulin spikes.
nutrition.catalogCarbsLocal: Cuts food miles and freight sharply, preserves the biodiversity of native seed and avoids the soil degradation of monoculture.

nutrition.catalogFatsItem2: Seeds in bulk: pumpkin seeds, chia, ground flaxseed and sesame.
nutrition.catalogFatsItem4: Artisanal 100 % peanut or almond butter, with no added sugar or oils.
nutrition.catalogFatsNutrition: They let you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, regulate the hormonal system and modulate the inflammatory response.
nutrition.catalogFatsLocal: They keep small regional processors going and can be bought in reusable glass jars, with no disposable plastic.
nutrition.catalogOilsItem1: Regional cold-pressed avocado oil, for medium-high heat.
nutrition.catalogOilsItem2: Extra virgin olive oil, raw or on low heat.
nutrition.catalogOilsItem3: Steam, air fryer, or homemade vegetable and bone broths.
nutrition.catalogOilsItem4: A well pre-heated cast iron or non-stick pan, with no added fat.
nutrition.catalogOilsNutrition: Thermal stability and fats that are not oxidised: less cellular stress and cardiovascular protection.
nutrition.catalogOilsLocal: Displaces ultra-processed food tinned or bottled in plastic, and cuts the transport footprint and industrial fat waste.

nutrition.includes2: Encouraging people to grow their own (urban gardens or permaculture cells).
nutrition.includes3: Building a setting where choosing healthy, fresh, nearby food is the easiest option.

nutrition.bridgeMovementTitle: With Movement: going to the market is already moving
nutrition.bridgeMovementBody: Walking or cycling to buy the week’s fresh food is at once this pillar’s sourcing and the other one’s engine-free trip. One journey counts for both.
nutrition.bridgeMindTitle: With Mind and Spirit: the table without screens
nutrition.bridgeMindBody: Dinner with no devices in sight is also that pillar’s window of silence, and the stretch where a real conversation fits without scheduling anything.

sleep.heading: Sleep and Deep Rest
sleep.subtitle: Sleeping to the rhythm of light again, not of screens.
sleep.lightHeading: The Invention of Electric Light (1879): The End of Natural Sleep
sleep.lightIntro: This is perhaps the harshest turning point for our brain. Before Thomas Edison and artificial light, our circadian rhythm — the internal clock — was perfectly in step with the sun.
sleep.changeText: Night stopped being dark. We could work, eat and socialise long after sunset.
sleep.impactText: The body stopped producing melatonin properly. We began stealing hours from rest, which set off the chronic stress and inflammation we now see everywhere.
sleep.processesHeading: How many processes depend on sleep?
sleep.processesIntro: Sleep takes part in many essential functions, not just one:
sleep.brainText: memory and learning, synaptic plasticity, emotional and mood regulation.
sleep.challengeIntro: Prepare your night and get daylight when your morning begins.
sleep.metabolismText: regulating spend and replenishment of energy, anabolism, cell maintenance and clearing the brain's «waste» (the glymphatic system).
sleep.immuneText: defence against infection, response to vaccines, and control of the inflammation tied to cancer, depression and cardiovascular disease.
sleep.cardiovascularText: blood pressure, glucose, stress hormones, appetite hormones, reproductive health.
sleep.homeostasisText: balance across organ systems, metabolism, and psychological and social state.
sleep.evidence: The scientific evidence shows that sleep is involved in practically every critical process of body and mind. It is not a luxury: it is the physiological base of attention, memory, emotional stability, metabolism, immunity and long-term cardiovascular health.
sleep.callout: This pillar is the ground floor of biological recovery. It is not just about «sleeping», but about improving your sleep hygiene so body and mind can properly repair themselves. At {brand}, the aim is for technology to help track and encourage routines that respect circadian rhythms.
sleep.hiddenCostHeading: The hidden cost of artificial light and 24/7 culture
sleep.hiddenCostIntro: Electric light and screens broke the oldest agreement your body had: that darkness meant sleep. Bright light at night holds melatonin back and makes the brain believe it is still midday. That is paid for three times over.
sleep.fragmentedText: Falling asleep takes longer and you lose deep and REM stages, the ones that repair tissue and clear waste from the brain. You sleep the same hours and rest less.
sleep.stimulantText: Accumulated fatigue gets covered with caffeine and sugar in the morning, and that same caffeine gets in the way of the following night’s sleep. The circle closes on its own.
sleep.lightPollutionText: Extra hours of electric light at home, and a neighbourhood night that never quite gets dark: light pollution also throws off the insects and birds that live nearby.
sleep.localSolutionHeading: The counterweight: syncing with light again
sleep.localSolutionText: You do not need to buy anything. Sun on your face on waking, warm low light at dusk, and a dark, cool room give back the signal your body has been waiting for all its life. It is the cheapest of the four pillars: almost all of it consists of switching things off.
sleep.sanctuaryIntro: Your bedroom teaches your brain what happens in it. If you work, argue and browse there, the bed stops being a cue to sleep and becomes one more place to be awake. Three conditions reverse that.
sleep.sanctuaryDarkBody: Full darkness, or as close as you can get: thick curtains, and standby lights on devices covered or off. Darkness is the one signal your body accepts without arguing.
sleep.sanctuaryCoolBody: To fall asleep, your body temperature has to drop by about a degree. A cool room with air moving does that work for you; a hot one blocks it no matter how tired you are.
sleep.sanctuaryPhoneBody: The phone charging outside the bedroom, and a separate alarm clock. This is not willpower: it is putting physical distance between you and the midnight scroll, and between you and the notifications waiting when you open your eyes.
sleep.unloadIntro: Your head does not switch off with the light. Whatever is unfinished keeps taking up room —an open task is remembered better than a completed one— and that is exactly what goes round and round once your head hits the pillow.
sleep.unloadHowBody: Before bed, write down what you have pending for tomorrow and what is worrying you. You do not have to solve it or tidy it: getting it out of your body and onto paper you can come back to tomorrow is what lets your head let go. And make it what is pending, not what you already did: when this was measured in a lab, the people who wrote their to-do list fell asleep sooner than the ones who wrote up what they had achieved that day.
sleep.unloadCalmBody: Slow breathing, some light reading on paper or a caffeine-free infusion. Anything that tells your nervous system the day is over and there is no need to stay alert.
sleep.catalogIntro: What to do, what it does for your body and what it does for your electricity bill and the neighbourhood night.
sleep.catalogLightItem1: Stepping into the yard, the balcony or the street for 10 to 15 minutes on waking.
sleep.catalogLightItem2: Having breakfast or coffee next to an open window.
sleep.catalogLightItem3: Watching the sunset or walking for a while late in the afternoon.
sleep.catalogLightItem4: Going out without sunglasses in that stretch, never looking straight at the sun.
sleep.catalogLightBody: Sets the body clock, lifts your mood in the morning and schedules the following night’s melatonin.
sleep.catalogLightLocal: Brings life onto the street at the hours the neighbourhood is awake, and saves artificial light during the day.
sleep.catalogEnvironmentItem1: The phone charging outside the bedroom, with a separate alarm clock.
sleep.catalogEnvironmentItem2: Warm, low light at home from dusk onwards.
sleep.catalogEnvironmentItem3: Thick curtains and device lights covered or switched off.
sleep.catalogEnvironmentItem4: The bed only for sleep and intimacy; work stays out.
sleep.catalogEnvironmentBody: Raises your own melatonin, cuts late-hour stimulation and shortens the time it takes you to fall asleep.
sleep.catalogEnvironmentLocal: Lowers the household’s electricity use and adds less spilled light to the community’s night.
sleep.catalogUnloadItem1: Five minutes of unloading into a notebook before bed.
sleep.catalogUnloadItem2: A hot caffeine-free infusion: chamomile, lemon balm, linden.
sleep.catalogUnloadItem3: Slow breathing, letting the air out gently without forcing.
sleep.catalogUnloadItem4: A paper book beside the bed instead of the phone.
sleep.catalogUnloadBody: Frees your head of what is pending, stops rumination and slows the pulse so you get into bed calm.
sleep.catalogUnloadLocal: Leans on plants you can buy in bulk and in season, rather than on one more packaged purchase.
sleep.bridgeHeading: How the other three pillars arrive here
sleep.bridgeIntro: Rest is where everything else is settled up. And these are not extra tasks: the three bridges already exist on the other pages, and here is where you find out whether they were kept.
sleep.bridgeNutritionBody: An early dinner lets digestion finish before bed, and does not get in the way of the drop in body temperature deep sleep needs.
sleep.bridgeMovementTitle: From Movement: moving by day and outdoors
sleep.bridgeMovementBody: Moving during the day builds up the sleep pressure that makes your body ask for rest at dusk, and outdoor light reinforces the same clock that anchors your morning.
sleep.bridgeMindTitle: From Mind and Spirit: the last hour screen-free
sleep.bridgeMindBody: The mental unload and the digital close calm the nervous system, so you get to bed without your head still running.

mindSpirit.cardDescription: Health is not only physical. This pillar centres on emotional care, mental clarity, connection with others —starting with whoever lives nearby— and a sense of purpose. Keeping healthy relationships and feeling part of something larger drives the other three pillars.
mindSpirit.description: Silence, presence and real bonds with the people nearby
mindSpirit.title: Mind, Spirit and the Community Next Door

movement.cardDescription: It is not limited to the gym, and it does not exclude it either: it covers walking, cycling, playing, working the land or training at a neighbourhood studio. The aim is for movement to fit back into the day, with your local surroundings as the place where it happens.
movement.description: Getting movement back on the street, the trail and the neighbourhood pitch
movement.title: Natural, Local, Community Movement

nutrition.cardDescription: More than a diet, this pillar encourages real food: minimally processed, varied, seasonal and locally sourced. It builds the bridge between farmers and the people who eat, and creates a setting where choosing healthy food is the easiest option.
nutrition.description: A connection to the source: local, fresh, real food
nutrition.title: Natural, Nourishing, Local Food

sleep.cardDescription: Sleep is not a luxury: it is the physiological base of attention, memory, emotional stability, metabolism, immunity and cardiovascular health. Improving your sleep hygiene is the first step towards letting body and mind repair themselves properly.
sleep.description: Better sleep hygiene, so your body can actually recover
sleep.title: Sleep and Rest

pillarsOverview.whyBody: Modern science confirms what ancestral wisdom already knew: restorative sleep, natural food, daily movement and connection with our community are the foundations of a healthy life. Each pillar reinforces the others, creating a virtuous circle of whole wellbeing.
